ruleName: Divots, tractor ruts, bald patches, etc.
title: Playing from a divot, rut or bald patch
question: Your ball lands in a deep divot or a tractor rut on the fairway. Which of these is correct?

choices.text: You must play the ball as it lies or take an unplayable lie and add a penalty
You can move the ball to some good grass without penalty
You are allowed to rehit your shot with no penalty

explanation: You have to play the ball as it lies, or declare it unplayable and take a penalty stroke—there is no free relief just for a divot or rut.

juniorVersion.title: What if your ball is in a hole or bumpy spot?
juniorVersion.question: Your ball lands in a deep hole made by someone’s shot or a track from a tractor on the fairway. What should you do?

choices.text: You must hit the ball as it is, or say it’s unplayable and take a penalty.
You always get to move your ball for free.
You can pick up your ball and put it on the nice grass for free.
You can hit again from the same place without a penalty.

juniorVersion.explanation: You need to hit the ball where it is, even if it’s in a hole or tractor mark. If you don’t want to play it, you can say it’s unplayable, but you have to add a penalty.

vocabulary.simpleMeaning: A hole or chunk taken out of the grass by someone’s golf club.
When your ball is in a spot too hard to play, and you say so, but you get a penalty.
The short grass between where you start and the green.

juniorVersion.teachingTip: Show kids what a divot or tractor rut looks like on the course. Ask them to try playing a shot from a divot so they understand how tricky it can be.
likelyMisconceptions: Some children may think they can always move their ball out of a hole or bump for free.
They might believe deep ruts are like puddles, where you get free relief.
